doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Codified material, wrong notes and the colors of jazz
summary: He explains coloring outside the lines, using all 12 notes, and likening non-chord tones to Bach and Parker.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you think it’s harder for a young player today to find an original sound because they have so much codified material to draw from.

Well you have to realize that the codified material is half of it, and the other half is sort of the primal part of you, the creative part of you that wants to take that vocabulary or that lexicon and then play it in a very non-academic way. So if you could be Jekyll and Hyde in the sense that two different people, in order to get across what you want to get across. But yeah, there’s a lot of players out there that forget about that other half, they’re very academic about it and they say well the book says to play this particular scale over this particular chord so they do that. And they sound correct. But I think in any art it’s not enough to sound correct or look or be correct. It’s when we start coloring outside the lines, that’s when I think a person’s creativity is really explored. And unless you do that you will always play correctly but you won’t necessarily be as creative as you should be, I think, in art. So I think one should color within the lines first, which is what my book’s about, and then you’d have all that knowledge and material and then take that material and start coloring outside the lines. So I think personally that’s the avenue I took and I’m glad I did.
So are there wrong notes in improvising?

Well — no, no, no. It’s basically you have a choice of all 12 notes of the chromatic scale. It’s a good thing we don’t live in the Middle East where they have 48 notes and 96 notes. I mean we think we have it difficult in Europe and the Americas, and now in the Middle East where they have micro-tunings in India, it’s got to be extremely difficult and their

minds are just rife with information. We’ve got 12 notes, and they can all be used. But where are they used and how are they used is, at this point — at that point when you understand how to play through chord changes, the harmonies, then it’s all about not what notes all the time, but how to use the notes and where to put those notes. So in answer to your question I think that’s sort of what I did. I could play perfectly and play just the notes I need to play, but then the other chromatic tones are very important too, like they are in J.S. Bach’s music. It’s the same vocabulary. We have names for notes that didn’t really fit in the chords as appoggiaturas and —

and escape tones, which are known as echappées, and upper neighbors and lower neighbors, and grupettos and all that. In jazz it’s the same thing. You know Charlie Parker didn’t call it that, but it’s exactly the same thing.
Yeah. We call it after he played it.

Exactly. Yeah. And those are the colors of jazz, those notes. You know it’s like taking a black and white painting, which is sometimes beautiful, and then once in a while throw in some red, some blue, throw on some green. And those are those notes that we might not be allowed to play but we could make sense out of those notes so it’s how we play them and where we play them that really give your composition — which it is a composition — color. A jazz solo is a composition, a spontaneous composition but nevertheless a composition, and sometimes we need more color.
